newsitem.title: USA: Ameritech to refile long distance bid by end of Q1.
newsitem.headline: Ameritech to refile long distance bid by end of Q1.

text.p: Ameritech Corp expects by the end of March to refile its application with regulators to become the first Baby Bell to enter the $80 billion long distance telephone market, the company's chairman said Wednesday.
Richard Notebaert told reporters he expects the filing will happen "probably" before the end of the first quarter. "It's not tomorrow."
The Chicago-based carrier was forced to withdraw its landmark request earlier this month after the U.S. Federal Communications Commission said that critical documents filed by Ameritech were flawed.
In particular, the FCC said Ameritech had not submitted a finalized agreement showing that the carrier had opened its local phone network in Michigan to AT&T Corp.
Ameritech asked the FCC on January 2 for permission to offer long-distance service to residents in Michigan, one of five midwestern states in which it provides local service.

Under last year's telecommunications act, Ameritech and the other regional Baby Bells must prove to regulators that they have opened their local phone monopolies to new competitors before gaining access to the long-distance market.
Ameritech officials said that before they can refile their application, Michigan regulators must formally approve the company's "interconnection" agreement with AT&T.

This would involve Michigan officials issuing a formal document as well as an order saying that the agreement has been approved and is consistent with an arbitration accord struck between the two companies last November.
Ameritech officials were confident that once Michigan regulators took these steps, their application to enter the long-distance business from the state would be approved by the FCC.
Notebaert said that unless the FCC's goal were to prevent the Bells from entering the long-distance market, "this should go quite smoothly."
Notebaert declined to be specific about the company's long distance plans after Michigan. He did note that Ameritech has made the most progress with regulators in Wisconsin and Illinois.
